title: Pathophysiology: Hematologic Function & Systemic Shock—Oxygen Delivery, Hemostasis, DIC and Multiorgan Failure
html:
Blood links every organ system. Red blood cells carry oxygen, leukocytes defend against infection, platelets and coagulation proteins limit blood loss, and plasma transports water, electrolytes, nutrients, hormones, medications, and waste. When oxygen-carrying capacity, hemostasis, circulating volume, cardiac output, vascular tone, or cellular oxygen use fails, localized disease can become systemic shock and multiorgan dysfunction.

Learning goals

  • Connect hemoglobin, cardiac output, and saturation to tissue oxygen delivery.
  • Classify anemia by production, loss, or destruction and by red-cell size.
  • Recognize hemolysis, marrow failure, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and thrombotic risk.
  • Explain primary and secondary hemostasis and fibrinolysis.
  • Distinguish bleeding from clotting disorders and explain why DIC causes both.
  • Compare hypovolemic, distributive, cardiogenic, and obstructive shock.
  • Recognize compensated shock before hypotension appears.
  • Prioritize restoration of oxygen delivery, cause control, and serial reassessment.

Oxygen delivery depends on more than pulse oximetry

Systemic oxygen delivery is the product of cardiac output and arterial oxygen content. Arterial oxygen content depends mainly on hemoglobin concentration and hemoglobin saturation, with only a small contribution from oxygen dissolved in plasma. A client can therefore have a normal pulse-oximeter value but inadequate oxygen delivery because of severe anemia or low cardiac output.

Tissues normally extract part of delivered oxygen. When delivery falls, the body can increase heart rate, contractility, ventilation, vascular tone, and oxygen extraction. These compensations have limits and increase myocardial workload. Persistent imbalance between oxygen delivery and demand produces cellular dysfunction, anaerobic metabolism, lactate generation in some settings, acidosis, endothelial injury, and organ failure.

A normal SpO₂ does not guarantee adequate tissue oxygenation
Pulse oximetry estimates the percentage of hemoglobin binding sites occupied by oxygen; it does not report how much hemoglobin is present or whether circulation delivers it to tissues.

Anemia is a problem of oxygen-carrying capacity

Anemia reflects insufficient circulating red-cell mass or hemoglobin for physiologic need. Severity depends on the hemoglobin level, speed of change, cardiopulmonary reserve, oxygen demand, and cause. Gradual anemia may permit compensation, while rapid blood loss can produce shock before the hemoglobin concentration fully reflects the loss.

Organize anemia by mechanism: reduced production, blood loss, or increased destruction. Reticulocytes help assess marrow response. A low or inappropriately normal reticulocyte response suggests impaired production; an elevated response can accompany blood loss or hemolysis when marrow capacity and required nutrients are intact.

Mean corpuscular volume adds a second lens. Microcytic patterns commonly involve impaired hemoglobin synthesis, including iron deficiency or thalassemia. Normocytic patterns include acute blood loss, inflammation, kidney disease, or early nutrient deficiency. Macrocytic patterns include vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, medication effects, alcohol-related disease, liver disease, hypothyroidism, or marrow disorders. Size is a clue, not a final diagnosis.

Iron, vitamin B12, folate, kidney function, and marrow all matter

Iron is required for heme synthesis. Chronic blood loss is an important cause of iron deficiency and should prompt investigation rather than replacement alone. In inflammation, iron may be sequestered and erythropoietin response blunted even when body iron stores are present.

Vitamin B12 and folate are required for DNA synthesis. Deficiency can cause ineffective erythropoiesis and macrocytosis; vitamin B12 deficiency can also produce neurologic injury. Kidney disease reduces erythropoietin production and may shorten red-cell survival. Marrow infiltration, aplasia, medications, toxins, infection, or malignancy can reduce one or multiple cell lines.

Pancytopenia means red cells, leukocytes, and platelets are all reduced. The resulting cluster—fatigue or dyspnea, infection risk, and bleeding—should be interpreted as possible marrow or systemic disease rather than three unrelated problems.

Hemolysis destroys red cells faster than they can be replaced

Hemolysis may occur within the circulation or in the spleen and liver. Causes include immune reactions, membrane or enzyme defects, hemoglobin disorders, infection, toxins, mechanical shear, and microangiopathic processes. Findings can include rising indirect bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase, reduced haptoglobin, reticulocytosis, jaundice, dark urine, splenomegaly, and characteristic smear findings.

Severe hemolysis can cause abrupt anemia, kidney injury, hyperkalemia, and circulatory instability. In sickling disorders, deoxygenation, dehydration, acidosis, inflammation, and vascular adhesion promote polymerization and vaso-occlusion, creating ischemic pain and organ injury. The mechanism is not simply a low hemoglobin value.

Leukocytes defend, but count alone does not equal function

Neutrophils provide rapid defense against many bacterial and fungal infections. Neutropenia reduces the inflammatory response, so serious infection may produce fever with few local signs. The absolute neutrophil count is more useful than the total leukocyte count for estimating neutropenia severity.

Leukocytosis can reflect infection, inflammation, stress, glucocorticoids, tissue injury, or malignancy. A high count does not prove infection, and a normal count does not exclude it. In an immunocompromised client, fever, hypotension, new confusion, tachypnea, or subtle site findings require prompt evaluation.

Hemostasis is a controlled sequence

Vessel injury triggers vasoconstriction and exposure of subendothelial structures. Platelets adhere, activate, and aggregate to form the primary plug. The coagulation cascade generates thrombin, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin and stabilizes the plug. Natural anticoagulant pathways limit extension, while fibrinolysis later breaks down fibrin.

Platelet-number or platelet-function disorders often cause mucosal bleeding, petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, or prolonged oozing. Coagulation-factor disorders more often produce deep-tissue bleeding, large ecchymoses, hemarthrosis, or delayed rebleeding. These patterns overlap, especially in severe or mixed disorders.

Tests must be interpreted in context. Platelet count does not measure platelet function. PT/INR and aPTT sample parts of the coagulation system but do not independently predict all bleeding or clotting risk. Medication exposure, liver function, kidney function, fibrinogen, D-dimer, smear, bleeding pattern, and trends help complete the picture.

Thrombosis reflects Virchow's triad

Venous and arterial thrombosis arise when procoagulant influences exceed anticoagulant and fibrinolytic control. Virchow's triad organizes risk into stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability. Immobility, surgery, cancer, pregnancy, estrogen exposure, prior thrombosis, inflammation, vascular devices, and inherited conditions can combine.

Venous thrombi commonly cause unilateral swelling, pain, warmth, or may be silent; embolization can cause sudden dyspnea, chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, syncope, or shock. Arterial occlusion threatens tissue distal to the blockage and may present with sudden pain, pallor, pulselessness, weakness, sensory change, or coldness. Do not massage a limb when acute thrombosis is suspected.

DIC causes clotting and bleeding at the same time

Disseminated intravascular coagulation is secondary to a severe trigger such as sepsis, major trauma, obstetric catastrophe, malignancy, or extensive tissue injury. Systemic coagulation activation deposits fibrin in the microcirculation, consumes platelets and coagulation proteins, activates fibrinolysis, and injures organs. The client can therefore develop both thrombosis-related ischemia and diffuse bleeding.

Concerning findings include oozing from puncture sites, petechiae, ecchymoses, mucosal or internal bleeding, cool or mottled digits, altered mentation, oliguria, respiratory deterioration, and shock. Common laboratory trends include falling platelets and fibrinogen, prolonged coagulation times, elevated fibrin-degradation markers, and fragmented red cells. No single result diagnoses every case.

Treatment centers on controlling the underlying trigger while supporting perfusion and replacing blood components when clinically indicated. Repeating laboratory and clinical assessment is essential because DIC evolves rapidly.

Shock means inadequate cellular perfusion

Shock is circulatory failure in which oxygen delivery or use does not meet tissue demand. Blood pressure can remain temporarily normal through tachycardia and vasoconstriction; hypotension is often a later finding. Evaluate mental status, skin temperature and perfusion, pulse quality, capillary refill, urine output, respiratory effort, acid–base status, lactate trend, and organ function alongside pressure.

Mean arterial pressure is influenced by cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance. Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. Preload, contractility, afterload, rhythm, vascular tone, circulating volume, and mechanical obstruction all shape the hemodynamic pattern.

Four major shock mechanisms guide hypotheses

  • Hypovolemic shock: Hemorrhage or fluid loss reduces preload and stroke volume. Compensation increases heart rate and vascular resistance; extremities are often cool and pulses narrow or weak.
  • Distributive shock: Pathologic vasodilation and altered distribution reduce effective perfusion. Sepsis, anaphylaxis, and neurogenic mechanisms differ, but low vascular resistance is central. Early septic shock may have warm skin and bounding pulses despite dangerous maldistribution.
  • Cardiogenic shock: Pump failure reduces forward flow while filling pressures and congestion may rise. Myocardial infarction, severe dysrhythmia, myocarditis, or acute mechanical failure can cause the pattern.
  • Obstructive shock: A mechanical barrier prevents cardiac filling or output. Massive pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, and cardiac tamponade require rapid cause-specific relief.

Mixed shock is common. For example, sepsis can combine vasodilation, capillary leak, relative hypovolemia, and myocardial dysfunction. A client with hemorrhage and preexisting heart failure may not tolerate a generic resuscitation approach.

Compensation can conceal deterioration

Sympathetic activation redistributes blood toward the heart and brain, activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and antidiuretic hormone, and reduces kidney and skin perfusion. Tachycardia, anxiety, cool skin, delayed refill, thirst, reduced urine, or a narrowing pulse pressure can precede hypotension. Older adults, athletes, pregnant clients, clients taking rate-limiting medications, and those with autonomic dysfunction may not show a typical heart-rate response.

As compensation fails, myocardial perfusion falls, endothelial permeability increases, microcirculatory flow becomes heterogeneous, and acidosis impairs vascular responsiveness and contractility. This creates a cycle of worsening perfusion. Restoration of a blood-pressure number without improved mentation, urine output, skin perfusion, lactate trend, and cause control does not prove recovery.

Lactate is useful, but not a stand-alone diagnosis

Lactate may rise when oxygen delivery is inadequate, but adrenergic stimulation, impaired clearance, medications, seizures, and other mechanisms can also increase it. A normal early lactate does not exclude regional ischemia or compensated shock. Interpret the direction of change with the clinical picture rather than using one threshold as a substitute for assessment.

Multiorgan dysfunction is an interacting network failure

Persistent shock and inflammation injure endothelium and mitochondria, disrupt capillary flow, increase permeability, and activate coagulation and immune pathways. The lungs may develop permeability edema, kidneys acute injury, liver metabolic and synthetic dysfunction, brain encephalopathy, gut barrier failure, and heart depression. Dysfunction in one organ increases stress on the others.

Prevention depends on early recognition, restoring oxygen delivery without causing avoidable overload, controlling hemorrhage or infection, relieving obstruction, supporting failing organs, preventing secondary injury, and reassessing response. Treatment must match the mechanism: fluid alone cannot correct every shock state, and raising vascular resistance without addressing volume, pump failure, or obstruction may worsen harm.

Treat the mechanism, not just the monitor
A pressure reading, hemoglobin result, platelet count, or lactate value is one part of the picture. The priority is whether tissues are being perfused and whether the underlying cause is being controlled.

Translate hematologic and shock physiology into clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify bleeding, bruising, clot symptoms, infection risks, medication exposure, disease trajectory, mental status, work of breathing, perfusion, urine output, CBC and reticulocytes, smear, coagulation tests, fibrinogen, metabolic findings, lactate, and organ trends.
  2. Analyze cues: Link findings to impaired cell production, loss, destruction, platelet dysfunction, factor deficiency, thrombosis, consumption, low volume, vasodilation, pump failure, obstruction, or mixed shock.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Active hemorrhage, transfusion reaction, febrile neutropenia, DIC, pulmonary embolism, acute arterial occlusion, and any form of shock outrank stable chronic abnormalities.
  4. Generate solutions: Plan ABC support, monitoring, access, blood-bank and laboratory preparation, infection or hemorrhage control, cause-specific shock therapy, organ support, and escalation.
  5. Take action: Activate emergency pathways, protect the airway, support oxygen delivery and circulation, stop a suspected harmful infusion when appropriate, implement prescribed therapy, and coordinate definitive source control.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Trend mentation, respiratory status, pressure and pulse pattern, skin perfusion, urine output, bleeding, thrombosis signs, CBC, coagulation, fibrinogen, acid–base status, lactate, and organ function.

Clinical example

A client with severe infection becomes confused and tachypneic, with warm mottled skin, falling blood pressure, reduced urine output, oozing from venipuncture sites, falling platelets and fibrinogen, prolonged coagulation times, and rising D-dimer. The RN recognizes distributive shock complicated by DIC rather than interpreting the bleeding as an isolated platelet problem. Priorities are rapid ABC and perfusion support, sepsis and source-control measures, serial coagulation and organ assessment, prescribed blood-component support when clinically indicated, and evaluation of response across the entire cue cluster.
